srcs.episode: Health Issues of Musicians

podcast.title: Bipolar Disorder Misdiagnosis and Medication
podcast.body: Matthew Good was initially on antidepressants (Thexer) for anxiety, but his general practitioner increased the dosage. Higher dosages of this drug are known to amplify mania in individuals with bipolarity. This, combined with being given Ativan to counteract the mania, led to him taking up to 12 Ativan pills a day. "He up the dosage of a drug called a thexer that I was on. And one of the things that it does is it hired dosages. It amplifies mania and people who suffer from bipolarity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians With Disabilities

podcast.title: Bipolarity Diagnosis and Dysphoric Mania
podcast.body: While on antidepressants (a drug referred to as "Effexor" or "fixer" in the transcript) for anxiety, an increased dosage inadvertently amplified an undiagnosed bipolarity. He identified his condition as Type 1 bipolarity, eventually leading to dysphoric mania—a state of intense manic energy combined with a depressive state, which he described as "worse than a nuclear weapon" due to its overwhelming suffering and high associated suicide rate. "Now bipolarity is a genealogical disorder, which means you have it from birth."

podcast.title: Comparison to Jeff's "I'll Break Your Heart"
podcast.body: Matthew Good referenced the song "I'll Break Your Heart" by "Jeff" (presumably Jeff Buckley), where the artist throws up in a stall, to illustrate his own intense physical illness and vomiting before vocal takes during the recording of the `Audio of Being` album. "it's kind of like, you know, I'll break your heart. You know, where Jeff just goes into the stall and just throws up."

podcast.title: Divorce and Cocaine Incident
podcast.body: Matthew Good experienced a sudden divorce involving "a great deal of betrayal," including the post-fact discovery that his ex-wife had hidden a suitcase of cocaine in their house for a friend under investigation, an act he was unaware of at the time. He stated he had not drunk for 11 years and never really done drugs. "When you find out after the fact that your ex-wife brought a suitcase of cocaine into your house to hide because some guy she knew was under investigation for dealing it, and you don't know that at the time. Bit of a deal breaker."

podcast.title: Early Career Success
podcast.body: Matthew Good began his fruitful multi-decade career in the very late 1980s or early 1990s, establishing himself as one of the prominent "stars" during Canada's 1990s music boom. He is noted as a long-term survivor in the music business, indicating sustained relevance and activity over several decades. "Our lady piece, Matthew Good...had fruitful multi-decade careers that began in either the very late 1980s or the early 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Musical Start
podcast.body: Matthew Good began his musical journey unexpectedly at the very end of high school, having never sung before. He was asked to write lyrics for a folk band that played acoustic guitars. To learn singing, he listened to Simon & Garfunkel's "Bookends" multiple times and mimicked the vocals. This initial folk phase eventually evolved into a rock band. "I'd never sang before in my life and some guys were in a folk band and well, look, folk band, they played acoustic guitars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Edgefest Performer
podcast.body: Matt Good was one of the Canadian artists who performed at Edgefest during its national run from 1997 to 1999, which primarily showcased Canadian talent. "Arlady Pieces, I'm other Earth, finger-11, gobslone, Matt Good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 8: The CanRock Revolution

podcast.title: Fine Art School & Economic Hardship (Early 90s)
podcast.body: Matthew Good briefly attended fine art school but dropped out due to the severe economic climate of the early 1990s recession and his family's financial situation. He then took a job at a gas station, working long hours from 5:30 AM to 5:00 PM, considering himself fortunate to have it. During this period, he was on welfare for six months and encountered many people facing extreme hardship, such as a woman in Port Moody from Nova Scotia with no family, struggling to care for her baby. "I dropped out of school and went back and got a job and to help out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Geneological Bipolarity and Dysphoric Mania
podcast.body: Matthew Good recognized his bipolarity as a genealogical disorder present from birth, noting past behaviors like being on Ritalin at age 7 and experiencing periods of not sleeping for three or four days in his 20s, which he later identified as mania. In his 30s, he began suffering from dysphoric mania, a severe state combining manic energy with depressive states, which he described as "hell." "But when you get into your 30s, I started suffering from dysphoric mania, which is not like a happy, jubilant mania. It's more kind of akin to being put in a coffin with the two things you fear most, buried underground, and then having that coffin shrink in the time is, you know, times up by about a thousand. It's health, and you're awake for it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians With Disabilities

podcast.title: Hospitalization and Enlightenment
podcast.body: During a manic episode while in Bristol, England, Matthew Good returned home and, in an accidental overdose of sedatives (referred to as "Ativan" or "out of Ann" in the transcript) combined with alcohol, collapsed. He woke up in the hospital, where he willfully committed himself for about a week. This period, facilitated by cooperative hospital staff and a familiar psychiatrist, led to a "mass enlightenment" about his condition, marking it as a "cathartic experience." "I woke up in the hospital and I had to willfully commit myself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Intense Anxiety and Illness During Recording
podcast.body: During the recording of the `Audio of Being` album, Matthew Good experienced severe anxiety and was physically ill, throwing up daily for eight months. This period was marked by his sarcoidosis and the worsening internal dysfunction of the Matthew Good Band, making the entire recording process a "nightmare." "Well, I threw up that entire year, every day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Juno Award Disdain
podcast.body: Matthew Good won two Juno Awards, including one for Best Video, but consciously chose not to attend the ceremonies. He views award shows as "counterproductive," comparing them to judging the relative greatness of painters like Chagall, Rothko, and Kandinsky, and expressed discomfort with how they are marketed as the "Canadian experience." "I didn't go the year I won. I didn't go the year I won one for best video. And it's okay. My mom's got them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Learning Guitar & Songwriting (Age 20)
podcast.body: At the age of 20, Matthew Good picked up a guitar for the first time. He taught himself about four or five open chords and immediately began writing his own songs, rather than learning others' material. His early compositions were simple, often using E minor C progressions with many verses, reflecting his admiration for Bob Dylan. "I picked up a guitar for the first time and I taught myself about four or five open chords and I started writing songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Manic Episode and Hospitalization
podcast.body: While in Bristol, England, with plans to write a book in France, Matthew Good experienced a complete manic episode. Following an incident at his parents' townhouse involving alcohol and Ativan, he hit the floor and subsequently woke up in the hospital, where he willfully committed himself for about a week. His psychiatrist happened to be from his old neighborhood, which facilitated his cooperative engagement with the process, leading to an "enlightenment" about his condition. "I woke up in the hospital and I had to willfully commit myself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians With Disabilities

podcast.title: Personal Crisis and Divorce
podcast.body: Matthew Good experienced a "dark" period in his personal life following a sudden and traumatic divorce. This event was compounded by a sense of "betrayal," including the discovery that his ex-wife had hidden a suitcase of cocaine in their home, an action linked to a friend's legal troubles. "Well, I got divorced. And that was a sudden thing. Yeah, it was a very, very sudden thing. And there was a great deal of betrayal involved in it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Personal Struggles & Band Breakup
podcast.body: Matthew Good reflects on carrying a lot of guilt, admitting that an illness he had might have been the true reason the band broke up, or that it contributed to him being perceived as difficult in the media or by those close to him. He acknowledges these as possibilities that play a role in his past, stating that to deny them would be ignorant. "It wasn't me, it was the fact that I had an illness that was at the reason the band broke up or was I difficult or did I characterize this difficult in the media or with people that were for me because of that reason."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Can Rock Revolution Survival
podcast.body: Matt Good's career continued successfully long after the 1990s, indicating the enduring impact of the Can Rock Revolution. "Many acts survived long after the decade ended. The tragically hip, Sloan, R80p, Serma Glockland, Tea Party, Matt Good, many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 8: The CanRock Revolution

podcast.title: Recovery and Outpatient Care
podcast.body: After his hospitalization, Matthew Good went through a process of outpatient care to find a suitable drug regimen to manage his bipolar disorder. This period marked a significant turning point in understanding and addressing his long-standing mental health challenges. "And then you go through the process of outpatient care and finding a drug regime that works for you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians With Disabilities

podcast.title: Retrospective on Career
podcast.body: Matthew Good often looks back at his past work and thinks "what the hell was I thinking" rather than feeling immense pride. He reflects on carrying guilt for many things, acknowledging that an illness might have been a factor in his band's breakup or in being characterized as difficult. "I think I probably look back more and think what the hell was I thinking."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Sarcoidosis Diagnosis
podcast.body: Matthew Good suffered from sarcoidosis, a disease that progressively affects different parts of the body, and for him, specifically his lungs. It causes lung tissue to turn into scar tissue over time, making it difficult to breathe, a condition also experienced by Bernie Mack. Matthew uses an inhaler but has avoided steroid treatments like prednisone due to their severe side effects. "Sarcoid osus. It's basically a disease that can affect different parts of your body. For me, it affects my lungs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Self-Reflection on Band Breakup
podcast.body: Matthew Good expressed ongoing guilt and self-doubt regarding the Matthew Good Band's dissolution, questioning whether his undiagnosed illness, his perceived "difficult" personality, or media portrayals of him contributed to the split. He acknowledged these as possibilities and felt it would be ignorant to deny his potential role. "I think I probably look back more and think what the hell was I thinking."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Edgefest Panda Incident (1999)
xref.body: During the Matthew Good Band's performance on the main stage at Edgefest in Wilson Park, Barrie, in 1999, Universal Music marketing representative Iber Hamilton, dressed in a giant panda costume, attempted a stage dive during the song "Everything's Automatic." From the 10-12 foot high stage, he launched into the crowd, which unexpectedly parted "like the Red Sea." The panda landed face down on the ground 12 feet below, suffering a bleeding nose (his head was protected by a football helmet within the costume) and was subsequently kicked by some members of the audience. Matthew Good, performing with his microphone back by the monitor lines, did not immediately see what happened but later found Hamilton in the back with a bloody face. This incident later inspired the artwork for the "Loser Anthem" EP. "The crowd parts like the Red Sea. Everybody moves. Panda, bam! Face down on the ground, 12 feet below the stage."

xref.title: Breakup in 2001
xref.body: The Matthew Good Band dissolved around 2001, an outcome of pervasive internal dysfunction, Matthew's illness, and an unwillingness to tour the `Audio of Being` record. The band members had reached a point where communication broke down, and individuals asserted their indispensability, leading Matthew, who usually tried to "placate" others, to finally end the group. "And that was the end of the Matthew Good Band."

xref.title: Accidental Overdose Discussion
xref.body: Matthew Good's personal experience with an accidental overdose prompted a discussion about Nick Drake's death, which is also attributed to an accidental overdose of pills. Conflicting accounts exist, with some suggesting Drake took too many pills at once, while others propose he took a second pill after an initial dose wore off, leading to a fatal combination. "Wasn't this something that Nick Drake had?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

xref.title: Band Name Evolution (Matthew Good Band vs. MGB)
xref.body: The band initially used the acronym "MGB" on the first 5,000 copies of their debut album, "Last of the Ghetto Astronauts." However, public demand at radio (for "Alabama Motel Room") and retail led people to consistently request "Matthew Good Band." Faced with this popularity, the decision was made to officially adopt Matthew Good's name for the band, partly because early members were not fully committed and often had other academic pursuits. This event, however, was later described as "the beginning of the end" due to escalating ego issues. "The decision was made that that's what we would call it."

xref.title: Bipolar Disorder
xref.body: A significant factor in Scott Weiland's and Mary Forsberg's struggles was their undiagnosed bipolar disorder, which led to extreme mood swings and poor judgment, often exacerbated by self-medication with drugs like crack. Doctors initially misdiagnosed him with severe depression, and the treatments did not control his manic episodes. "A big part of their problems coping with life is that they were both undiagnosed sufferers of bipolar disorder, and this is a really important part of our story."

xref.title: Frequent Vancouver Performances
xref.body: Matthew Good recalled that the Dead Kennedys frequently played in Vancouver during his childhood in the 1980s. Their regular appearances highlight the city's once vibrant and influential music scene, which he believes has since lost its "edge." "I can't count how many times a day Kennedy's came to town when I was a kid, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Gil Norton's Production Work
xref.body: Producer Gil Norton had previously worked on the first few Foo Fighters albums and was committed to producing another Foo Fighters record in 1997, which prevented him from producing The Matthew Good Band's "Underdogs" album. "He had been doing the first few fighters albums by that point. He was just about to do color, didn't he? And that's why he couldn't do it. He couldn't do the record because he was doing the food record, and he'd already committed, but he really wanted to do it."

xref.title: Improvisational Genius Comparison
xref.body: Matthew Good cited Thelonious Monk as an example of musical genius and a reference for live-off-the-floor recording. He described a famous image of Monk changing music on the fly at his piano, with 17 session musicians observing over his shoulders to capture the evolving changes without any written notation. "It always reminds me of that famous picture of Philoneast Monk."

xref.title: Internal Dysfunction and Political Dynamics
xref.body: The Matthew Good Band suffered from significant internal dysfunction, described as "very political and weird," particularly during the creation of `Audio of Being`. This included members vying for publishing rights by injecting ideas and a general lack of communication during tours, ultimately contributing to the band's dissolution. "It might have been even more successful had the Matthew Good band been functioning properly. There was a lot of internal dysfunction."

xref.title: Musical Influence on Matthew Good
xref.body: Matthew Good considered himself a "Dylan maniac," and his early songwriting, characterized by simple chord progressions like E minor C with many verses, was heavily influenced by Bob Dylan. "I mean, I'm a, you know, I'm a Dylan maniac so, you know, that's the way it was, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

xref.title: Musical Influence on Matthew Good
xref.body: The Pixies were a significant influence on Matthew Good's songwriting, particularly in their approach to the bass guitar. He noted their use of the bass as a "straight A instrument" that moved in steps, which contrasted with the more melodic bass lines of 60s and 70s music he also admired. "But also someone that was massively influenced by bands like The Pixies and the Replacements and Afghan Wigs and that kind of things. It was a straight A instrument."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Matthew Good listened "a lot of Buddy Holly" while developing his 2004 album `White Light Rock and Roll Review`. This influence contributed to his decision to record the album in a primitive, "live off the floor" style, emulating classic recording techniques. "I had been listening to like a lot of Buddy Holly"

xref.title: Notable Clients
xref.body: The studio has attracted a wide array of prominent artists from around the world, including The Offspring, Slayer, The Tragically Hip, Three Days Grace, Metallica, AC/DC, R.E.M., Matthew Good, Nickelback, and Muse (who recorded their 2015 album *Drones* there). "Warehouse studios has been very popular with some big names from all over the world."

xref.title: Post-Breakup Member Activities
xref.body: Following Age of Electric's original run, members pursued various projects: the Dahle brothers formed Limblifter, Todd Kerns became the bass player and backup vocalist for Slash in The Conspirators, and three other members joined Matthew Good's backup band. These transitions highlight the interconnectedness of Canadian musicians. "Todd Kerns from Age of Electric has been working as the bass player in Back of Vocalist for Slash, yes, as in Guns and Roses Slash, in his band The Conspirators."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

xref.title: Post-Name Change Ego Struggles
xref.body: The formal adoption of "The Matthew Good Band" name led to significant ego issues within the group, which Matthew Good described as "the beginning of the end." To maintain peace and cohesion, he made efforts to placate other members, even going as far as to give up publishing rights and credit that he felt wasn't necessarily due. "From that day forward, ego was about everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

xref.title: Top Billing Misperception
xref.body: The band was publicly perceived as primarily "Matthew Good," giving him top billing despite his personal preference against it. This public misperception was a factor in the band's identity and internal dynamics. "The Matthew Good Band was a group that gave Matt top billing, something that he never wanted. This all came as the result of a public misperception."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
